title: Stream Framing and Eviction Safety Spec
content:
Abstract:
This spec introduces a frame-based streaming model for generation outputs that focuses on safe flush boundaries, predictable cancellation and preemption, and KV-cache eviction safety. It describes a runtime-compatible framing format, flush heuristics, kernel preemption hooks, and a KV-cache commit/rollback model to ensure correctness under concurrent scheduling and eviction.

Motivation:
Current token-streaming approaches either emit sub-token bytes or eager token-level outputs with inconsistent semantics around partial tokens and cache side-effects. This results in subtle application-level behavior: downstream systems receive partial tokens that later change, and KV cache updates become visible before we can safely roll back on cancellation or preemption. We need a clear contract so that consumers (SDKs, server-sent events, websockets) and internal schedulers can reason about correctness, latency, and resource eviction.

Design goals:
- Deterministic flush boundaries that can be described to clients (so they can show partial output but know when parts are final).
- Minimal extra latency: flush heuristics should hit typical UI latency targets (~50ms) without excessive tokenization churn.
- Safe KV cache semantics: ability to rollback or isolate speculative outputs until a commit point.
- Kernel-friendly preemption points to avoid long uninterruptible execution blocks.
- Backwards-compatible fallbacks and incremental rollout.

Core concepts:
1) Frame: the unit of streaming emission. A frame contains:
   - frame_id: monotonic per-request integer
   - seq_offset: token-index offset into the output sequence
   - tokens: list of fully-closed tokens (may be empty)
   - partial: optional byte/chunk representing an in-progress token fragment (string")
